title: Bibi Amro
hook: Guru Angad's daughter whose dawn singing brought Amar Das to the Guru

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baba Buddha, the boy who met Guru Nanak and, tradition says, lived long enough to serve one Guru after another. Your line was six gurus served. Did someone's long faithfulness come to mind? Today, a song before sunrise. Day eight hundred seven.

It's still dark. In a village house a young woman sits at the churn, pulling the cord back and forth, turning milk into butter the way it was done every morning. And while her hands work, she sings. Not loudly. Just enough to keep time with the churn. On the other side of the wall, an older man in the same family is awake too. He's a devout man, and tradition says he has walked to the holy river many times in his life, still looking for something. He hears the words. He stops what he's doing. And he asks a question that will change the rest of his life: whose words are these? Today: Bibi Amro.
screen: `STILL DARK, A CHURN, A SONG.` → `AN OLDER MAN LISTENING.` → `WHOSE WORDS ARE THESE?`

segments.voice: Bibi Amro was the daughter of Guru Angad, the second Guru, who sat in Guru Nanak's seat at Khadur. Tradition says she married into the family of a man named Amar Das, and went to live in his village. Amar Das was religious in the way of his time. He kept fasts, he went on pilgrimage, he was good and careful. But the story says he had never had a teacher. Then, one morning, he heard his young relative singing at her work. The song was a hymn of Guru Nanak. Tradition says the words went straight into him. He came to her and asked whose they were. She told him plainly: these are Guru Nanak's words, and my father now sits in his place. That's all she had to say. Amar Das asked her to take him there. So she did. She brought him to Khadur, to her father, and he never really left. The story says he stayed to serve Guru Angad, carrying water, doing the plain work of the house, for years. And in time, Guru Angad chose him to be the next Guru. Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. Now notice what Bibi Amro did, and what she didn't. She didn't argue with him. She didn't set out to convince anybody. She was churning butter. The song was part of her morning, as ordinary as the milk. And because it was real to her, it carried through a wall. Some people share what they believe by arguing for it. Sikhs remember Bibi Amro for sharing it the other way: it simply sounded while she worked. One woman, singing at dawn, and the Guruship found its next keeper.
screen: `A DAUGHTER OF GURU ANGAD.` · `A HYMN SUNG WHILE CHURNING.` · `TAKE ME TO YOUR FATHER.` · `FAITH THAT CARRIES THROUGH A WALL.` · then, large: `HER SONG CHANGED A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing something near someone. Not a performance. Just a quiet song while you do something with your hands. For this sit, start by settling. Let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one song or line you love, sacred or not. If you know a shabad, you can use that. Let it run quietly in your head, in time with the breath, the way Bibi Amro kept time with the churn. After the bell, if someone is nearby, hum it softly while you wash a cup or fold something. The bell holds the time.
Bibi Amro. Guru Angad's daughter, whose song at dawn, tradition says, brought Amar Das to the Guru. Today's word.

Your line: her song changed a life. Today, let something you love be heard in an ordinary moment, a hum in the kitchen, a line said aloud, without trying to make it mean anything. Day eight hundred seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bibi Amro in the story of how Guru Amar Das came to Guru Angad, and some Sikh households still sing gurbani during ordinary work, at home and at dawn.

fork.setup: you're Amar Das. before dawn you hear a young relative singing words that go straight into you. what do you do?
options: keep quiet and go on with your own pilgrimages.
ask her whose words these are.
correct her for singing so early.
fork.reveal: he asked, and she told him plainly: Guru Nanak's words. then he asked her to take him to her father, and his life turned.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Bibi Amro; Bibi is a respectful title for a woman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Guru's daughter, mentioned in passing.
what it means: the person whose ordinary morning song, tradition says, brought the future third Guru to the Guru's door.
what a scholar hears: the telling puts a household woman, singing gurbani at her work, at the hinge where the Guruship passes from Guru Angad to Guru Amar Das.

sources.ref: Bibi Amro and Amar Das, Sikh tradition

notes: Bibi Amro marrying into Amar Das's family (tradition: to his brother's son) and living in his village (Basarke): stated only as 'married into the family'; confirm.
Amar Das's earlier pilgrimages to the Ganges and his years of carrying water at Khadur are given as 'tradition says'; no counts or ages given on purpose.
The churn detail is from the common telling; some versions just say she sang at dawn. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with it.
Editor: howItsDone changed from 'part of many Sikh households' to 'some Sikh households' (claims rule).

Auditor: review's 'met Nanak' given his title (Guru Nanak); the narrator's contrast between 'faith that is mostly talk' and faith that 'leaks out' (a ranking of how people believe) reworded as a description of how Sikhs remember her.
